title: "Intermediate R"

## Explore data frames

Loading a dataset from NHSRdatasets

```{r}
data <- NHSRdatasets::ae_attendances

# or

data <- ae_attendances
```

## Looking at the column names

Get a `character vector` of column names

```{r}
colnames(data)
```

Show the data type

```{r}
class(colnames(data))
```

Prove this is a vector

```{r}
is.vector(colnames(data))
```

What are [vectors again](https://intro-r-rstudio.nhsrcommunity.com/session-vectors.html#/title-slide)?

## Looking at the data


Using base R the `$` helps to select a column 

In RStudio typing the data frame name then $ prompts with a drop down wizard

```{r}
data$type
```


Get a vector of unique data items in a variable

```{r}
unique(data$org_code)
```

## When is base R useful?

::: {.incremental}
- It's useful in packages where dependencies can cause long term maintenance issues.
- That's similar to data analysis too as packages may move in and out of CRAN
- Sometimes it's faster to run in analysis code
- Sometimes it's faster to read
- Some coding styles like `data.table` are much more similar to base R than dplyr so this can be a useful step to learning other packages

:::

## Finding specific data points

Particular data points can be extracted and these are where `[ ]` square brackets are used.

This gets the 4th entry  

```{r}
data$type[4]
```

We could also call the 4th to 10th entries  

```{r}
data$type[4:10]
```

## What does `Levels` mean?

::: {.incremental}
- The Levels for this data relates to it being a `factor` (categorical data) 
- The levels are showing what else is available
- A `factor` is a categorical variable (column of data) with a predefined list of allowed values
:::

## Over to you

Can you find the data type for the columns `period`, `org_code` and `attendances`?

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 7,
  color_border = "#005EB8",
  color_text = "#005EB8",
  color_running_text = "white",
  color_running_background = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_text = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_background = "white",
  margin = "0.9em",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```

## Answer - find data types

```{r}
class(data$period)
class(data$org_code)
class(data$attendances)
```

:::{.callout-caution collapse=false appearance='default' icon=true}
## Python user warning!
If you are a python coder (or will be in the future) it's worth knowing that R starts counting from 1 and not zero.
:::

## Other useful functions - distinct

```{r}
# remember this gets the unique values
unique(data$org_code)

# this counts them
n_distinct(data$org_code)
```


## Statistics functions

Get the range of a variable (useful for dates)

```{r}
range(data$period)
```

See structure of data to check data types (looks like the Environment panel in RStudio)

```{r}
str(data)
```

## Top and tail data

See the first 5 rows of data

```{r}
head(data)
```

See the last 5 rows of data

```{r}
tail(data)
```

See the first 15 rows of data

```{r}
head(data, 15)
```

## Using dplyr to top and tail


See the first 15 rows of data - but using dpylr

```{r}
dplyr::slice_head(data, n = 15)
```

See the first 15% of total rows of data (as it is currently with no ordering:

```{r}
dplyr::slice_head(data, prop = 0.15)
```

See the first 15% of total rows of data (grouped by type)

```{r}
dplyr::slice_head(data, prop = 0.15, by = type)
```


## Over to you

Find the lowest 5 attendances for each org code

Use the function `dplyr::slice_min` and don't forget the help documentation (F1 or search directly in the Help pane of RStudio)

If that's quick to solve try the lowest 5 attendances for org code _and_ type.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(
  minutes = 8,
  color_border = "#005EB8",
  color_text = "#005EB8",
  color_running_text = "white",
  color_running_background = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_text = "#005EB8",
  color_finished_background = "white",
  margin = "0.9em",
  font_size = "2em"
)
```


## Answer for lowest 5 attendances

For one category

```{r}
dplyr::slice_min(data,
  n = 5,
  order_by = attendances,
  by = org_code
)
```

For two categories

```{r}
dplyr::slice_min(data,
  n = 5,
  order_by = attendances,
  by = c(org_code, type)
)
```

## Looking at the structure of a data fram

`summary()` is a super function that also can give great summaries of other
objects - such as linear models

```{r}
summary(data)

```

## Quick counts by a column

```{r}
table(data$type)

```

or by 2 columns

```{r}
table(data$type, data$org_code)

```

You can do 3 columns but it starts to get silly how that is displayed!

## Outputting data into code

A handy little function

```{r}
smaller_data <- data |> 
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 1) |> 
  dplyr::select(period,
                org_code
                )

dput(smaller_data)
```

:::{.callout-note collapse=false appearance='default' icon=true}
## Factors are metadata
Notice how all the org codes are listed but there is only 1 row for `RF4`
:::
